In the warm, clear waters of the Indo-Pacific, the Chevron butterflyfish (Chaetodon trifascialis) exhibits a suite of life-history traits closely tied to its obligate corallivorous diet. Field surveys conducted at a stable water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] have documented that the pelagic eggs, which measure approximately 0.75 millimeters in diameter, hatch after a remarkably short developmental period. From these tiny, yolk-sac larvae, the newly emerged prolarvae are estimated to have a wet weight at birth of just 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], a minimal mass that reflects the limited endogenous reserves provided by the small egg. The age at birth, meaning the duration from egg fertilisation to eclosion, has been recorded as approximately 1.3 days [ab = approximately 1.3 days] under these same ther at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]mal conditions. This rapid hatching time is characteristic of many tropical reef teleosts and is considered an adaptation to reduce the vulnerability of the embryonated egg to pelagic predators during the earliest, most defenseless developmental stage.

The species reaches a relatively modest ultimate total length compared to many of its butterflyfish congeners, with the maximum recorded size in the wild plateauing at 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters]. Individual growth trajectories, derived from extensive mark-recapture data on the Great Barrier Reef, indicate that somatic expansion is rapid during the first year of benthic life before decelerating markedly as the fish approaches this asymptotic body size. This ultimate length places Chaetodon trifascialis among the smaller members of its genus, a morphology that may facilitate its exploitation of narrow crevices within branching coral thickets for shelter and foraging. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is estimated at 108 grams [Wwi = 108 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions that describe the species' robust, laterally compressed body form. This adult mass is attained only after several years of steady growth on the coral reef.

The onset of reproductive capability in the Chevron butterflyfish is tied to the attainment of a specific body size. Detailed histological analyses of gonadal tissue from preserved museum specimens indicate that individuals first become capable of reproducing once they reach a total length at puberty of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters]. At this size threshold, which roughly corresponds to the end of the juvenile phase, the gonads begin to show clear signs of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the established length-weight relationship for this species, is approximately 9.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.9 grams]. Achieving this body mass appears to be a critical energetic prerequisite, allowing the fish to divert resources away from continued somatic growth and toward the costly process of gamete production. This size-based maturity schedule is common among iteroparous coral-reef fishes.

Reproductive output in Chaetodon trifascialis has been quantified through field-based sampling of spawning aggregations and subsequent histological determination of batch fecundity. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) peaked at an average of 6% [GSI = 6%] for gravid females sampled at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. These continuous spawning events are thought to offset the low survival probability of individual pelagic larvae in a resource-poor open-ocean environment, thereby ensuring that at least some offspring encounter suitable settlement habitat on the reef.

Longevity data for the Chevron butterflyfish, gathered from both otolith-based age estimates and long-term photographic monitoring of tagged individuals on protected reef slopes, suggest a maximum lifespan of just over 25 years [am = just over 25 years] when measured at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, which is considerable for a small-bodied reef fish, is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy that allows repeated reproductive opportunities across many seasons. The ability to persist for such a long duration is likely tied to the species' highly specialised diet, which minimises competition with generalist herbivores, and its well-developed antipredator morphology, including the prominent dorsal and anal spines that deter potential gape-limited predators on the reef. Natural mortality in older adults is typically attributed to senescence-related decline in physiological condition, leading eventually to a post-reproductive death.
